questions.question: Prove that √2 is irrational.
questions.answer: Assume √2 is rational. Then √2 = p/q for some integers p, q with q ≠ 0 and HCF(p, q) = 1 (we can always reduce to lowest terms). Squaring: 2 = p²/q², so p² = 2q². Hence p² is even, which means p is even (an odd integer's square is odd). Write p = 2k. Then p² = 4k² = 2q², so q² = 2k². So q² is even, hence q is even. But then both p and q have a common factor 2, contradicting HCF(p, q) = 1. So our assumption is wrong, and √2 is irrational. Q.E.D.

questions.question: Prove that 5 + 3√2 is irrational, given that √2 is irrational.
questions.answer: Suppose 5 + 3√2 is rational. Let 5 + 3√2 = r where r is rational. Then 3√2 = r − 5 (rational − rational = rational, so RHS is rational). So √2 = (r − 5)/3 — but rational/rational = rational. This says √2 is rational, contradicting the given. Hence 5 + 3√2 is IRRATIONAL.

questions.question: Without performing the division, decide whether each fraction has a TERMINATING or NON-TERMINATING-REPEATING decimal expansion: (a) 7/8, (b) 13/3125, (c) 64/455, (d) 23/30.
questions.answer: (a) 7/8: 8 = 2³ → terminates (m=3, n=0). (b) 13/3125: 3125 = 5⁵ → terminates (m=0, n=5). (c) 64/455: 455 = 5 · 7 · 13. 64 = 2⁶. HCF(64, 455) = 1 (already in lowest terms). Denominator has 7 and 13 — NOT just 2's and 5's → non-terminating-repeating. (d) 23/30: 30 = 2·3·5. The 3 means non-terminating-repeating.
questions.explanation: Use the 2^m · 5^n test on the lowest-terms denominator.

questions.question: Three bells start ringing together at 7:00 a.m. They ring at intervals of 12 minutes, 15 minutes and 18 minutes respectively. (i) When will they next ring together? (ii) How many times will all three ring together in the next 6 hours?
questions.answer: (i) Need LCM(12, 15, 18). 12 = 2²·3; 15 = 3·5; 18 = 2·3². LCM = 2²·3²·5 = 180 minutes = 3 hours. Next together at 7:00 + 3:00 = 10:00 a.m. (ii) After 7:00 a.m., they ring together at 10:00 a.m., 1:00 p.m. (within 6 hours). That's 2 more times in the next 6 hours (from 7 to 13:00).

questions.question: Prove that √3 is irrational. (Use contradiction.)
questions.answer: Assume √3 is rational. Then √3 = p/q for some integers p, q with q ≠ 0 and HCF(p, q) = 1. Square both sides: 3 = p²/q², so p² = 3q². This means 3 divides p². Since 3 is prime, this implies 3 divides p (because if p had no factor of 3, p² wouldn't either). Write p = 3k. Then p² = 9k² = 3q², so q² = 3k². So 3 divides q² and hence 3 divides q. But then 3 is a common factor of p and q, contradicting HCF(p, q) = 1. So √3 is IRRATIONAL.
questions.explanation: Same structure as √2 proof, using the 'p prime divides p² means p divides number' rule.

questions.question: Two friends Aman and Bina jog around a circular track. Aman completes a round in 18 minutes; Bina in 24 minutes. They start jogging at 6 a.m. (i) When will they meet again at the starting point? (ii) Where in the day (morning / afternoon) will they meet? (iii) How would your answer change if a third friend, Chetan, jogs with a 30-minute round?
questions.answer: (i) Find LCM(18, 24). 18 = 2·3²; 24 = 2³·3. LCM = 2³·3² = 72 minutes = 1 hour 12 minutes. They meet again at 6:00 + 1:12 = 7:12 a.m. (ii) Morning. (iii) With Chetan added, find LCM(18, 24, 30). 30 = 2·3·5. LCM = 2³·3²·5 = 360 minutes = 6 hours. So all three meet again at 6:00 + 6:00 = 12 noon.
questions.explanation: Practical LCM problem with two and three numbers.
